title: Cold Email Isn't Dead: The 5 Fixes Guide (With the Data Behind Each One)
description: The 5 fixes behind our 82,671-email campaign: tracking off, small lists, verified lists, short emails and smart follow-ups. Plus a problem finder table and weekly checklist.
lead: This is the full 5 fixes guide from the reel. The reel showed 2 fixes. Here are all 5, why each one works, exactly how to do it, and a table to find what's wrong with your own campaign. These are the same fixes behind our 82,671 emails, 2,429 replies and 2,146 interested leads.
insider: These numbers are from our own agency client campaign (June 1 to October 19, 2026), with open tracking off the whole time. Only **6 of 76,081** people asked to be removed. You can copy the 5 fixes yourself. If you'd rather have them running next month without learning it all, that's exactly what we do.

blocks.text: First, what "normal" looks like

Before fixing anything, know the target. [Instantly's 2026 benchmark report](https://instantly.ai/cold-email-benchmark-report-2026) puts the average reply rate at **3.43%**. The top quarter of senders get **5.5% or more**, and the top 10% get **10.7% or more**. [Hunter's 2026 report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email) found a **4.5%** average, but only **3%** for sales emails. If you're under 1%, something below is broken.
Fix 1: Turn open tracking off

**Why:** open tracking adds a tiny hidden image to every email. Spam filters notice it, and it turns a plain-text email into an HTML one. In Hunter's data, campaigns with tracking **off got 7.4% replies vs 4.4% with it on**.
Open rates aren't even reliable anymore. Apple Mail and some security tools open emails automatically, so your "open rate" includes robots.

items: In your sending tool, turn off **open tracking** for every campaign.
Turn off **link tracking** too, or set up a custom tracking domain if you really need clicks.
Track what pays you instead: replies, interested replies and booked calls.

blocks.text: Fix 2: Send to smaller, tighter lists

**Why:** a small list forces you to write for one kind of buyer. In Hunter's data, campaigns sent to **21 to 50 people got 6.2% replies vs 2.4% for 500+ people**. The average campaign went to 449 people, so most senders are on the wrong side of this.
Hunter also found that emailing **1 or 2 people per company got 5.1% replies vs 3.5% for 3 or more**. Emailing the whole team at once looks like spam to them and to filters.

items: Split your big list by industry, job title, company size and location.
Inside each group, look for a shared trigger: hiring, new funding, a new location.
Write one version of the email for each small group, with a first line about what they have in common.
Contact 1 or 2 people per company, not 5.

blocks.text: Fix 3: Verify every email before you send
**Why:** bounces tell inbox providers you're emailing people you don't know. Hunter's average bounce rate was 3.6%. Keep yours **under 2%**. Above that, your other emails start landing in spam.

items: Run every list through an email verifier before it goes into a campaign, even a list you just bought.
Remove invalid addresses. Remove "risky" ones, or send them later from a separate small campaign.
Be careful with "catch-all" addresses (domains that accept everything). Send to them only in small batches and watch bounces.
Verify again if a list is more than a month or two old. People change jobs all the time.

blocks.text: Our own campaigns run between 0.45% and 3.08% bounce, and we pause any inbox that goes over the line until the list is cleaned.
Fix 4: Keep it short and plain
**Why:** busy people read email on their phone and decide in seconds. Instantly's 2026 report found the best campaigns keep emails **under 80 words**.

items: Under 80 words, so it fits on one phone screen without scrolling
Plain text: no images, no logos, no fancy design
No link in the first email, or one at most
One idea per email
End with one small question, like "Worth a look?", not "Can we book 30 minutes?"

blocks.label: Simple 4-line structure
blocks.text:
Line 1: something true about them (see our WELL guide)
Line 2: the problem that usually comes with it
Line 3: one proof that you fix it (a real result)
Line 4: a small yes-or-no question
Fix 5: Send smart follow-ups (and know when to stop)

**Why:** Instantly found that **58% of replies come from the first email** and **42% come from follow-ups**. Stop after one email and you lose almost half your replies. The same report found the best sequences are **4 to 7 emails, spaced 3 to 7 days apart**.

head: Email
Day
What to say
rows: The main email: about them, one result, small question.
A new angle: a different problem you solve, or a short case study.
Make it easy: offer something useful, like a short teardown or a free resource.
The polite close: "Should I stop reaching out about this?" These often get replies.

items: Never send "just bumping this up". Every follow-up needs a new reason to reply.
Reply in the same thread, so they can see the earlier email.
Stop immediately when someone replies, even with a "no".
Don't go past 7 emails. Each extra email adds more spam-report risk.

Bonus: send from a real domain

Hunter found emails from custom domains got **5.2% replies vs 2.5% from free addresses** like Gmail. Use separate domains that look like your brand, never your main domain. Our MATH guide shows how many you need.

blocks.text: Your weekly checklist

items: Open tracking and link tracking are off.
Every list sent this week was verified first.
Bounce rate is under 2% on every inbox.
Each campaign goes to a small group with one shared reason to care.
Every email is under 80 words and plain text.
Every follow-up has a new angle.
Interested replies get an answer the same day.

blocks.label: Bottom line
blocks.text: Cold email isn't dead. Bad cold email is.

faq.q: If tracking is off, how do I know it's working?
faq.a: Count replies, interested replies and booked calls. Those are the numbers that pay you anyway.
Around 3 to 4.5% is average, 5.5% or more is top-quarter and 10% or more is excellent, based on Instantly's and Hunter's 2026 reports. Track interested replies too, since a reply can also be a no.

faq.q: How many follow-ups is too many?
faq.a: Instantly's data points to 4 to 7 emails in total. We usually stop at 4 or 5, because spam-report risk grows with each extra email.
In the U.S., yes, if you follow CAN-SPAM rules. Our [legal guide](/blog/is-cold-email-legal.html) explains it in plain English. Other countries have their own rules.
